title: Two distinct gap structures in the mid-infrared optical conductivity of the Hubbard model
abstract: Mid-infrared (MIR) optical conductivities in cuprate superconductors show universal features. In this study, we demonstrate that these originate from two distinct gaps: the pseudogap mediated by antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations and the Mott-Hubbard gap. The MIR spectra from these two gaps show a characteristic and distinct shape and doping dependence, and can thus be distinguished. Specifically, the Mott-Hubbard correlations, while rendering a peak in the visible spectrum for small dopings, yield a broad optical response starting in the MIR when a ``waterfall'' develops in the one-particle spectrum at larger dopings. The numerically and analytically determined doping-dependence of both gaps consistently reproduce experiments, and provide a unified microscopic understanding of the cuprate MIR optical conductivity.
summary: This work theoretically explains the mid-infrared optical conductivity in cuprate superconductors by proposing that it originates from two distinct electronic gaps: the pseudogap from spin fluctuations and the Mott-Hubbard gap. Using the Hubbard model and DΓA calculations, the authors show that the characteristic spectral features can be uniquely attributed to each gap, providing a unified microscopic picture.
main_problem: The study aims to elucidate the origin and doping-dependence of the characteristic mid-infrared (MIR) optical conductivity peaks observed in cuprate superconductors.
main_result: The MIR optical conductivity arises from two distinct, yet intertwined, gaps: one from the pseudogap (PG) mediated by spin fluctuations, and another from the Mott-Hubbard gap structure (LHB-QPB waterfall).
method: The analysis employs the ladder dynamical vertex approximation (DΓA) applied to the Hubbard model, supplemented by semi-analytical modeling of the self-energy pole structure.
model_or_system: The system is the Hubbard model on a square lattice, relevant to cuprate superconductors, with parameters set to model the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital. The calculations use the Kubo formalism for optical conductivity.
key_observables:
Mid-infrared (MIR) optical conductivity ($\sigma(\omega)$), the nodal spectral function $A(\mathbf{k}, 
u)$, and the difference $\sigma(\omega) - \sigma_{	ext{Drude}}(\omega)$.
important_parameters: Doping level ($\delta$), Hubbard interaction ($U$), and the relative contributions from the PG and Mott-Hubbard gaps.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the DΓA approximation, and the PG gap structure is modeled as anisotropic s-wave, with its nodal gap being above the Fermi energy.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the evolution of the nodal spectral function and optical conductivity ($\sigma(\omega)$) across different doping levels, distinguishing the contributions from the PG structure and the LHB-QPB waterfall.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the MIR optical conductivity by identifying and modeling two distinct gap contributions—the PG and the Mott-Hubbard gap—and demonstrating how their characteristic shapes and doping dependencies can be separately reproduced by the theoretical framework.
why_interesting: The clear separation and microscopic understanding of spectral features arising from different correlation mechanisms (spin fluctuations vs. local correlations) provide a powerful theoretical tool for interpreting complex spectroscopic data in strongly correlated materials.
